headline: Record Wildlife Photography Competition Celebrates Nature's Complexity
meta_description: Italian photographer Federico Veronesi wins wildlife photographer of the year with a poignant image of a grieving elephant, as the competition reaches record e…
summary_short: A heartbreaking photograph of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won the top prize in the wildlife photographer of the year competition, which received a recor…
body:
Italian photographer Federico Veronesi has claimed the overall title of wildlife photographer of the year with his haunting image titled The Aftermath, which documents a female elephant carrying her dead calf in the Huab River Valley, Namibia. The photograph offers a rare glimpse into elephant behaviour and possibly demonstrates grief in animals—a discovery that resonates far beyond the technical mastery of its composition. The Natural History Museum's annual competition, now in its 62nd year, received a record-breaking 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories this year, reflecting growing global interest in wildlife photography as a tool for conservation and understanding. Kathy Moran, chair of the judging panel, described the winning image as both emotionally devastating and intellectually profound: "Emotionally it's a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually it's proof that animals have cognition."

The youth category winner, British photographer Oscar Whitfield, captured something equally remarkable in his award-winning shot Labour of Love—a dung beetle pushing a ball of dung across dusty ground in Zimbabwe, celebrating the extraordinary effort behind the insect's everyday survival. Remarkably, both the adult and youth overall winners were recognised for black and white images, a first in the competition's history.

Dr Doug Gurr, director of the Natural History Museum, emphasised the deeper significance of this year's winning selections: "Together they remind us that every species plays a role in the complex web of life, and why understanding and protecting the natural world has never been more important." An exhibition of the winning photographs launches on Friday 16 October at the museum, offering the public an opportunity to witness how photography can fundamentally reshape our perception of the natural world.
quick_facts: Italian photographer Federico Veronesi wins with elephant photograph
Youth winner: British photographer Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe-based
Competition in 62nd year, run by Natural History Museum
First time both winners honoured for black and white images
